Okay, so I'm trying to figure out what happens to a wooden log when it's burned. The options are A) It is completely destroyed., B) It is completely changed into heat energy., C) It changes into other types of matter and energy., and D) It physically changes into the gaseous phase.

First, I remember that when wood burns, it undergoes combustion. Combustion is a chemical reaction where wood reacts with oxygen. I think this reaction produces some kind of gas and maybe solid residue. I've heard that burning wood releases carbon dioxide and water vapor, which are gases. There's also ash left behind, which is a solid.

So, if the wood turns into gases and solids, that means it's changing into different types of matter. Also, when wood burns, it releases energy in the form of heat and light. That energy isn't just heat; it's also light, which is electromagnetic radiation. So, the energy isn't just heat energy, but also light energy.

Looking at the options, A says it's completely destroyed. That doesn't make sense because we have products like CO2 and ash. B says it's completely changed into heat energy. But we have more than just heat; there's also light and the solid ash. So B isn't correct either.

C says it changes into other types of matter and energy. That fits because the wood turns into gases (matter) and releases energy (heat and light). D says it physically changes into the gaseous phase. While most of the mass does become gas, the wood also leaves behind ash, so it's not just a phase change into gas. Plus, the energy released isn't just a phase change; it's an actual energy transformation.

So, the best answer is C because it accounts for both the change in matter (to gases and solids) and the release of energy (heat and light).
